content: An athletic trainer is a certified healthcare professional who specializes in the field of athletic training. This profession has been recognized as an allied healthcare profession by the American Medical Association (AMA) since 1990. Certified athletic trainers (ATCs) must meet a rigorous set of qualifications to obtain certification. In some states and jurisdictions, the title athletic trainer is not regulated, which allows individuals who are not certified by the Board of Certification (BOC) to use the title. However, certified athletic trainers meet or exceed the minimum standards established by the BOC. The BOC is an independent organization accredited by the National Commission for Certifying Agencies (NCCA), which is the accreditation arm of the National Organization for Competency Assurance (NOCA). To become a certified athletic trainer, individuals must complete an accredited athletic training education program, hold a baccalaureate degree (though over 70% of ATCs possess a master’s degree or higher), and pass the BOC Certification Exam. Additionally, all ATCs are required to participate in continuing education and provide documentation of their ongoing professional development. Accredited athletic training education programs are overseen by the Commission on Accreditation of Athletic Training Education (CAATE), which ensures that both the didactic and clinical components of the curriculum meet established standards. Currently, there are 357 accredited entry-level athletic training education programs. The practice and regulation of athletic training vary by state. Forty-four states have licensure or regulation for athletic trainers, recognizing them as healthcare professionals similar to physical therapists and occupational therapists. Athletic trainers practice under the direct supervision of licensed physicians. Efforts are ongoing to establish licensure in the remaining states. The field of athletic training is divided into six distinct practice domains: 1. Prevention 2. Clinical evaluation and diagnosis 3. Immediate care 4. Treatment, rehabilitation, and reconditioning 5. Organization and administration 6. Professional responsibility The CAATE oversees the curriculum standards for all accredited athletic training programs. These standards dictate the content of both the academic and clinical practice components of the educational program. Key content areas include: Risk management and injury prevention Pathology of injuries and illnesses Orthopedic clinical examination and diagnosis Medical conditions and disabilities Acute care of injuries and illnesses Therapeutic modalities Conditioning and rehabilitative exercises Pharmacology Psychosocial intervention and referral Nutritional aspects of injuries and illnesses Healthcare administration Professional development and responsibility Athletic trainers provide care to a diverse population, including amateur and professional athletes, individuals with musculoskeletal injuries, and those seeking strength, conditioning, fitness, and performance enhancement. They also treat other patients as designated by a physician. Services provided by athletic trainers occur in a variety of settings, such as: Athletic training facilities Schools (K-12, colleges, universities) Clinics Hospitals Physician offices Community facilities Workplaces (commercial and government) Military installations and veteran medical facilities Professional sports organizations Emerging settings for athletic training include surgical fellowship opportunities, with pioneering programs established at Emory Sports Medicine Center in Atlanta, Georgia, and the Steadman-Hawkins Clinic in Vail, Colorado. In relation to the Mitchell Report, which investigated allegations of doping in sports, there has been confusion regarding the role of athletic trainers. Brian McNamee, a central figure in the doping allegations, has been referred to as a trainer or sports trainer, leading some to mistakenly believe he is a certified athletic trainer. According to the National Athletic Trainers' Association (NATA) and the BOC, McNamee is not, nor has he ever been, a certified athletic trainer. To date, no certified athletic trainer has been implicated in the doping issues associated with the Mitchell Report or the individuals cited in its contents. The NATA has issued a position statement opposing doping and the illicit use of performance-enhancing substances.
